title: From a Carceral–Industrial Site to a Cultural and Creative Park: Memory Governance and Spatial Reproduction in the Culture-Led Regeneration of Dissonant Heritage—The Case of Hechai 1972
content:
Background: Industrial heritage is increasingly being reused for cultural consumption. However, sites embedded in difficult institutional histories also require the governance of difficult memories and the reorganisation of site narratives.
Methods: This study examines the transformation of the former Hefei Prison into Hechai 1972 Cultural and Creative Park. Using a qualitative, interpretive single-case study design, it analyses historical and policy documents, official and media texts, spatial materials, field observations, and interviews through the lenses of critical heritage studies, memory governance, and spatial production.
Results: (1) The findings show that industrial production was historically embedded within prison administration and the reform-through-labour system, whereas these attributes were reordered in contemporary public narratives. (2) Prison memory was retained through selective retention, low-intensity interpretation, targeted access, externalisation, and reframing. (3) Industrial memory was foregrounded but detached from prison institutions, labour relations, and historical actors, producing a de-institutionalised representation. (4) Urban industrial memory, nostalgia for everyday urban life, and cultural and creative consumption subsequently functioned as substitute narratives and were reproduced through exhibitions, commercial uses, visitor practices, and social media circulation. (5) The study therefore identifies an interlocking mechanism involving the ordering of heritage attributes, memory governance, narrative substitution, and spatial reproduction.
Conclusion: The study argues that material conservation alone cannot ensure interpretive integrity. Culture-led reuse requires a coherent and publicly accessible interpretive system that connects material remains with institutional history and historical actors. These findings clarify the mechanisms and ethical boundaries involved in the regeneration of dissonant heritage in China and offer insights relevant to comparable sites with difficult institutional pasts.
